$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$

$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & 12 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & -9 \\ -9 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{19}[\begin{aligned}10 & 9 \\ 9 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-21 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$  

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 2+0\cdot (-2)+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{8}{4\cdot 2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Question 1
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[1−1−1],a2=[1−11],x=[400].

a
π4
b
π2
c
π3
d
π8
e
π6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]A=[11−1−1−11]⟹AT=[1−1−11−11]. Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[11−1−1−11]⋅([1−1−11−11]⋅[11−1−1−11])−1⋅[1−1−11−11]⋅[400]=[11−1−1−11]⋅[3113]−1⋅[44]=[11−1−1−11]⋅18[3−1−13]⋅[44]=[11−1−1−11]⋅[11]=[2−20]

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=4⋅2+0⋅(−2)+0⋅042+02+0222+(−2)2+02=8168=84⋅22=12=22.
Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(22)=π4,

which is already an acute angle.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$  

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}x}{‖x‖‖{\text{proj}}_{S}x‖} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 2+0\cdot (-2)+0\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\frac{8}{4\cdot 2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[1−1−1],a2=[1−11],x=[400].

a
π4
b
π2
c
π3
d
π8
e
π6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]A=[11−1−1−11]⟹AT=[1−1−11−11]. Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[11−1−1−11]⋅([1−1−11−11]⋅[11−1−1−11])−1⋅[1−1−11−11]⋅[400]=[11−1−1−11]⋅[3113]−1⋅[44]=[11−1−1−11]⋅18[3−1−13]⋅[44]=[11−1−1−11]⋅[11]=[2−20]

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx.

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=x⋅projSx‖x‖‖projSx‖=4⋅2+0⋅(−2)+0⋅042+02+0222+(−2)2+02=8168=84⋅22=12=22.
Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(22)=π4,

which is already an acute angle.

solution.reasoning: Both spanning vectors lie in the plane u+v=0. Since they are linearly independent, they span that plane, whose normal is n=(1,1,0). The angle θ between x and the plane satisfies sin θ=|x·n|/(‖x‖‖n‖)=4/(4√2)=1/√2, so θ=π/4. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured to verify its key.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

Question 2
?

Find the acute angle between the vector x and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors {a1,a2}, where a1=[111],a2=[11−1],x=[2−11].

a

b
2π5
c
π3
d
π6

0

Correct
EXPLANATION

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[11111−1]⟹AT=[11111−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[11111−1]⋅([11111−1]⋅[11111−1])−1⋅[11111−1]⋅[2−11]=[11111−1]⋅[3113]−1⋅[20]=[11111−1]⋅18[3−1−13]⋅[20]=[11111−1]⋅14[3−1]=12[112]

The acute angle between x and S is the acute angle between x and projSx. Equivalently, it is the acute angle between x and any non-zero vector that is parallel to projSx. So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

x=[2−11] and 2projSx=[112].

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

cos⁡θ=2⋅1+(−1)⋅1+1⋅222+(−1)2+1212+12+22=366=12.

Therefore,

θ=arccos⁡(12)=π3,

which is already an acute angle.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

M=[20−2040−40]R2:=R2−2R1∼[20−200000]. In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=x3. Therefore, the general solution is [x3x2x3]=x2[010]+x3[101],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[010],[101]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

Given the vector x and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system. x=[015],{2x1−4x3=06x1−12x3=0

a
[−313]
b
[−224]
c
[−122]
d
[211]
e
[0−2−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[20−4060−120]R2:=R2−3R1∼[20−400000]. In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2,x3 are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get x1=2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x3x2x3]=x2[010]+x3[201],x2,x3∈R.

Consequently, B={[010],[201]} is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of x onto the solution space of the system:

projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx=[021001]⋅([010201]⋅[021001])−1⋅[010201]⋅[015]=[021001]⋅[1005]−1⋅[15]=[021001]⋅15[5001]⋅[15]=[021001]⋅[11]=[211]

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & 12 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & -9 \\ -9 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{19}[\begin{aligned}10 & 9 \\ 9 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-21 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & 12 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$

question.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}],\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2}-12{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 4 & 12 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-20 \\ 5 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & -9 \\ -9 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{19}[\begin{aligned}10 & 9 \\ 9 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}65 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-21 \\ 2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/8bd85835b1bb951df5773824b45f53527a4cda3c4e988f7b30f151e289d47459.png)

In the figure shown above, we know that 
$m∠A=m∠B.$
What is the measure of the angle $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the measure of the interior angle at $A.$ Then,

$$
m∠A=m∠B=x.
$$

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{110}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{110}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={70}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+x+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={110}^{∘} \\ x & ={55}^{∘}\,\end{aligned}
$$

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {110}^{∘} & =x+x \\ {110}^{∘} & =2x \\ {55}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/0729bbdc2bec04cee7be1f0be31a44648b05a2536f7e17002d1dab6e2f3500c6.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{127}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{127}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={53}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $∠A$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠A+{73}^{∘}+{53}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠A & ={180}^{∘}-{126}^{∘} \\ m∠A & ={54}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

  

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $m∠A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {127}^{∘} & =m∠A+{73}^{∘} \\ {127}^{∘}-{73}^{∘} & =m∠A \\ {54}^{∘} & =m∠A\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where an exterior angle at $A$ is ${119}^{∘}$ and an exterior angle at $C$ is ${103}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the interior angle $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a corresponding picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/6fc411e7715044257a6818fe63fb3b7bd212c22a2f3d279f282b2b7161be3ecc.png)

   

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at $B$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{119}^{∘}+{103}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {222}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={138}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{138}^{∘} \\  & ={42}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m∠B={42}^{∘}.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $B.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{73}^{∘}+m∠B & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B & ={180}^{∘}-{73}^{∘} \\ m∠B & ={107}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ {41}^{∘}+{107}^{∘}+2x & ={180}^{∘} \\ {148}^{∘}+2x & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={32}^{∘} \\ x & ={16}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

  

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m\angle{A} +m\angle{B} +m\angle{C} = 180^\circ$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠B}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at [math]B[/math]}}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠C.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠B}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at [math]B[/math]}}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠C \\ {73}^{∘} & ={41}^{∘}+2x \\ {32}^{∘} & =2x \\ {16}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given a triangle $\triangle ABC$, let the exterior angles at ${A}$ and ${B}$ be equal $120^\circ$ and $100^\circ,$ respectively. What is the measure of the angle $\angle C?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's start by drawing the corresponding triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/3e2698fe8e2e886127669b1e04f45499706750312b447ff0c73524f2de4ff2ce.png)

  

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at ${C}$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is $360^{\circ}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{120}^{∘}+{100}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {220}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={140}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{140}^{∘} \\  & ={40}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m\angle C = 40^\circ.$

tutorials.name: The Sum of Exterior Angles
tutorials.problem:
Yet another important fact about exterior angles is:

The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a triangle is always equal to $360^\circ.$

So, for the triangle below, we have 

$$
x+y+z = 360^\circ.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/22586791e1118a38a554deffaec3ac5b73eafc47eee4be2052c0949dde584cea.png)

To see why, first recall that the measure of an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the measures of the two non-adjacent interior angles. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =m∠B+m∠C \\ y & =m∠A+m∠C \\ z & =m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that the internal angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =(m∠B+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠B) \\  & =2m∠A+2m∠B+2m∠C \\  & =2(m∠A+m∠B+m∠C) \\  & =2({180}^{∘}) \\  & ={360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the measure of the interior angle at $A.$ Then,

$$
m∠A=m∠B=x.
$$

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{110}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{110}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={70}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+x+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={110}^{∘} \\ x & ={55}^{∘}\,\end{aligned}
$$

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {110}^{∘} & =x+x \\ {110}^{∘} & =2x \\ {55}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

In the figure shown above, we know that m∠A=m∠B. What is the measure of the angle A?

a
35∘
b
50∘
c
55∘
d
45∘
e
70∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x be the measure of the interior angle at A. Then, m∠A=m∠B=x.

Method 1

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at C. We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

110∘+m∠C=180∘m∠C=180∘−110∘m∠C=70∘

Now, we calculate x using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180∘:

m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘x+x+70∘=180∘2x=110∘x=55∘

Method 2

We could rewrite the equation m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘ as

180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B.

Substituting, we can solve for x: 180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B110∘=x+x110∘=2x55∘=x

tutorial.name: The Sum of Exterior Angles
tutorial.problem:
Yet another important fact about exterior angles is:

The sum of the measures of the exterior angles of a triangle is always equal to $360^\circ.$

So, for the triangle below, we have 

$$
x+y+z = 360^\circ.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/22586791e1118a38a554deffaec3ac5b73eafc47eee4be2052c0949dde584cea.png)

To see why, first recall that the measure of an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the measures of the two non-adjacent interior angles. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =m∠B+m∠C \\ y & =m∠A+m∠C \\ z & =m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that the internal angles of a triangle sum to $180^\circ.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =(m∠B+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠C)+(m∠A+m∠B) \\  & =2m∠A+2m∠B+2m∠C \\  & =2(m∠A+m∠B+m∠C) \\  & =2({180}^{∘}) \\  & ={360}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/8bd85835b1bb951df5773824b45f53527a4cda3c4e988f7b30f151e289d47459.png)

In the figure shown above, we know that 
$m∠A=m∠B.$
What is the measure of the angle $A?$
question.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the measure of the interior angle at $A.$ Then,

$$
m∠A=m∠B=x.
$$

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{110}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{110}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={70}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+x+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={110}^{∘} \\ x & ={55}^{∘}\,\end{aligned}
$$

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {110}^{∘} & =x+x \\ {110}^{∘} & =2x \\ {55}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

In the figure shown above, we know that m∠A=m∠B. What is the measure of the angle A?

a
35∘
b
50∘
c
55∘
d
45∘
e
70∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x be the measure of the interior angle at A. Then, m∠A=m∠B=x.

Method 1

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at C. We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

110∘+m∠C=180∘m∠C=180∘−110∘m∠C=70∘

Now, we calculate x using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180∘:

m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘x+x+70∘=180∘2x=110∘x=55∘

Method 2

We could rewrite the equation m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘ as

180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B.

Substituting, we can solve for x: 180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B110∘=x+x110∘=2x55∘=x

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the measure of the interior angle at $A.$ Then,

$$
m∠A=m∠B=x.
$$

*Method 1*

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at $C.$ We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

$$
\begin{aligned}{110}^{∘}+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-{110}^{∘} \\ m∠C & ={70}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate $x$ using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to ${180}^{∘}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+x+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={110}^{∘} \\ x & ={55}^{∘}\,\end{aligned}
$$

*Method 2*

We could rewrite the equation $m∠A+m∠B+m∠C={180}^{∘}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\,=m∠A+m∠B.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{{180}^{∘}-m∠C}_{⏟}}_{\text{Exterior angle at }C}\,\,\, & =m∠A+m∠B \\ {110}^{∘} & =x+x \\ {110}^{∘} & =2x \\ {55}^{∘} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider a triangle △ABC, where the measure of an exterior angle at C is equal to 127∘ and m∠B=73∘. What is the measure of the angle A?

a
54∘
b
57∘
c
51∘
d
52∘
e
56∘
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by drawing the corresponding triangle.

Method 1

Let's start by finding the value of the missing interior angle at C. We use the fact that the interior and exterior angles are supplementary:

127∘+m∠C=180∘m∠C=180∘−127∘m∠C=53∘

Now, we calculate ∠A using the fact that the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180∘: m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘m∠A+73∘+53∘=180∘m∠A=180∘−126∘m∠A=54∘

Method 2

We could rewrite the equation m∠A+m∠B+m∠C=180∘ as

180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B.

Substituting, we can solve for m∠A:

180∘−m∠C⏟Exterior angle at C=m∠A+m∠B127∘=m∠A+73∘127∘−73∘=m∠A54∘=m∠A

question.worked_solution:
Since the exterior angles of a triangle sum to ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{80}^{∘}+(x-{20}^{∘})+x & ={360}^{∘} \\ 2x+{60}^{∘} & ={360}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={300}^{∘} \\ x & ={150}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where an exterior angle at $A$ is ${119}^{∘}$ and an exterior angle at $C$ is ${103}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the interior angle $B?$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a corresponding picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/6fc411e7715044257a6818fe63fb3b7bd212c22a2f3d279f282b2b7161be3ecc.png)

   

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at $B$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{119}^{∘}+{103}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {222}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={138}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{138}^{∘} \\  & ={42}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m∠B={42}^{∘}.$

feedback.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where an exterior angle at $A$ is ${119}^{∘}$ and an exterior angle at $C$ is ${103}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the interior angle $B?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a corresponding picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/6fc411e7715044257a6818fe63fb3b7bd212c22a2f3d279f282b2b7161be3ecc.png)

   

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at $B$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{119}^{∘}+{103}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {222}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={138}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠B & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{138}^{∘} \\  & ={42}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m∠B={42}^{∘}.$

solution.reasoning: The interior angles at A and B are 180°−100°=80° and 180°−122°=58°. Therefore C=180°−80°−58°=42°, choice a. The captured worked solution concerns a different example, so Math Academy's current answer key is not established.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: Consider a triangle $△ABC$, where an exterior angle at $A$ is ${100}^{∘}$ and an exterior angle at $B$ is ${122}^{∘}.$ What is the measure of the interior angle $C?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a corresponding picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191822/assets/b1d04d90855560e36762d492f34ac14fb960c98f55c234da7c706e638fd9ea9e.png)

   

Let $z$ be the measure of the exterior angle at $C$ pictured above. Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is ${360}^{∘}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{100}^{∘}+{122}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ {222}^{∘}+z & ={360}^{∘} \\ z & ={138}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠C & ={180}^{∘}-z \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{138}^{∘} \\  & ={42}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $m∠C={42}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/a3af5c931067f960d2099efdb9a19e23dd2835a16095cdc0e61a0a507b0e8a3c.png)

What is the domain of the function $f$ defined by the mapping diagram above?
questions.worked_solution:
The domain is the set of all input values for which the function is defined. In the mapping diagram, this corresponds to the set of values in the "Input" set:

$$
\{5,10,15,20\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/4091e1bee1b036185a54499839b356f8fce38e864d8f390915e855b26130e998.png)

What is the domain of the function $f(x)$ given above?
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ above is defined for values between $x=1$ and $x=4.$

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=1,$ this point is included in the domain.

- On the other hand, because there is an open circle at $x=4,$ this point is not included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
1\le x<4.
$$

Using interval notation, we write this as

$$
x\in [1,4).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Finite Domain of a Function From Its Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the domain of the function shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/16ee469ac79597e3afc65844e27a156fd45d8cbd3234f2fdc74e0ab9b4554237.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function above is defined for values between $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=-2,$ this point is included in the domain.

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=2,$ this point is also included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
-2 \leq x \leq 2.
$$

Using interval notation, we can write this as

$$
x \in [-2,2].
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function above is defined for all values of $x$ that are less than $x = 3.$

Therefore, the domain of this function is $x \leq 3,$ which we can write as $x \in (-\infty, 3].$

tutorials.name: Functions Defined on Closed Intervals
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the function $f(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/2a666cbc79869f13f7079db92396ae6f7ad2b2041b2aa0ea704149119a850eed.png)

Note the following:

- The function is not defined for $x<0,$ nor is it defined for $x > 2.$

- The function has filled circles at $x=0$ and $x=2,$ so it is defined at both of these points.

- In addition, the function is defined for every value of $x$ between $0$ and $2.$

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
0 \leq x \leq 2.
$$

We can also express the domain using interval notation:

$$
x\in [0,2]
$$

The square brackets $[\:]$ indicate that the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ are included in the domain.

tutorials.name: Functions Defined on Open Intervals
tutorials.problem:
Now consider the function $y=g(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/c99d3cbb1b7ba516cc2cf75856aeb17b9f91d23185d6fd25319a492ca4e3b164.png)

Note the following:

- The function is not defined for $x<0,$ nor is it defined for $x > 2.$

- The function has open circles at $x=0$ and $x=2,$ so it is *not* defined at either of these points.

- However, the function is defined for every value of $x$ between $0$ and $2.$

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
0 \lt x \lt 2,
$$

which we can write using interval notation as

$$
x\in (0,2).
$$

The parentheses $(\:)$ indicate that the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ are excluded from the domain.

tutorials.name: Functions Defined on Semi-Open Intervals
tutorials.problem:
It's possible for a function to have one endpoint included in the domain and another endpoint excluded. 

For example, consider the function is $y=h(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/0919c9b416ad49ed08d566b8c85d250a1a00a3ebf72f4d22c3d608fb42ede169.png)

The endpoint $x=-2$ is included in the domain, but the endpoint $x=2$ is excluded. Therefore, the domain of $h(x)$ is

$$
-2 \leq x \lt 2,
$$

which we can write using interval notation as

$$
x\in[-2, 2).
$$

tutorials.name: The Domain of a Function Given as a Graph
tutorials.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/a2660977b21e476e1a295e215ac22888625763b12b1685521c289adf8326f78c.png)

No matter which number $x$ we pick as an input, $f(x)$ always will return an output. Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as 

$$
x\in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Let's compare this to the function $g(x) = \dfrac 1 x,$ shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/84fefed3d54e57467ca3ebcf823c6bbf5c3c6aacce2f7542230b1abacfd97f46.png)

We cannot substitute the value $x=0$ into the function $g(x)$ because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, $x=0$ is not part of the domain of $g(x).$ However, we can use any other number $x$ as input for $g(x).$ Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ is

$$
x\in (-\infty, 0)\cup (0,\infty).
$$

This notation means that any number *apart from zero* can be used as an input for $g(x).$
tutorials.content:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/a2660977b21e476e1a295e215ac22888625763b12b1685521c289adf8326f78c.png)

No matter which number $x$ we pick as an input, $f(x)$ always will return an output. Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as 

$$
x\in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Let's compare this to the function $g(x) = \dfrac 1 x,$ shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/84fefed3d54e57467ca3ebcf823c6bbf5c3c6aacce2f7542230b1abacfd97f46.png)

We cannot substitute the value $x=0$ into the function $g(x)$ because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, $x=0$ is not part of the domain of $g(x).$ However, we can use any other number $x$ as input for $g(x).$ Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ is

$$
x\in (-\infty, 0)\cup (0,\infty).
$$

This notation means that any number *apart from zero* can be used as an input for $g(x).$

tutorial.problem:
Let's consider the function $f(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/2a666cbc79869f13f7079db92396ae6f7ad2b2041b2aa0ea704149119a850eed.png)

Note the following:

- The function is not defined for $x<0,$ nor is it defined for $x > 2.$

- The function has filled circles at $x=0$ and $x=2,$ so it is defined at both of these points.

- In addition, the function is defined for every value of $x$ between $0$ and $2.$

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
0 \leq x \leq 2.
$$

We can also express the domain using interval notation:

$$
x\in [0,2]
$$

The square brackets $[\:]$ indicate that the endpoints $x=0$ and $x=2$ are included in the domain.

It's possible for a function to have one endpoint included in the domain and another endpoint excluded. 

For example, consider the function is $y=h(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/0919c9b416ad49ed08d566b8c85d250a1a00a3ebf72f4d22c3d608fb42ede169.png)

The endpoint $x=-2$ is included in the domain, but the endpoint $x=2$ is excluded. Therefore, the domain of $h(x)$ is

$$
-2 \leq x \lt 2,
$$

which we can write using interval notation as

$$
x\in[-2, 2).
$$

tutorial.name: The Domain of a Function Given as a Graph
tutorial.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=2x,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/a2660977b21e476e1a295e215ac22888625763b12b1685521c289adf8326f78c.png)

No matter which number $x$ we pick as an input, $f(x)$ always will return an output. Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as 

$$
x\in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Let's compare this to the function $g(x) = \dfrac 1 x,$ shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/84fefed3d54e57467ca3ebcf823c6bbf5c3c6aacce2f7542230b1abacfd97f46.png)

We cannot substitute the value $x=0$ into the function $g(x)$ because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, $x=0$ is not part of the domain of $g(x).$ However, we can use any other number $x$ as input for $g(x).$ Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ is

$$
x\in (-\infty, 0)\cup (0,\infty).
$$

This notation means that any number *apart from zero* can be used as an input for $g(x).$

What is the domain of the function $f$ defined by the mapping diagram above?
question.worked_solution:
The domain is the set of all input values for which the function is defined. In the mapping diagram, this corresponds to the set of values in the "Input" set:

$$

$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192268/assets/4091e1bee1b036185a54499839b356f8fce38e864d8f390915e855b26130e998.png)

What is the domain of the function $f(x)$ given above?
question.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ above is defined for values between $x=1$ and $x=4.$

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=1,$ this point is included in the domain.

- On the other hand, because there is an open circle at $x=4,$ this point is not included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
1\le x<4.
$$

Using interval notation, we write this as

$$
x\in [1,4).
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

What is the domain of the function f(x) given above?

a
x∈[1,5)
b
x∈(1,5]
c
x∈[1,4)
d
x∈(1,4]
e
x∈[1,4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) above is defined for values between x=1 and x=4.

  • Since there is a closed circle at x=1, this point is included in the domain.

  • On the other hand, because there is an open circle at x=4, this point is not included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

1≤x<4.

Using interval notation, we write this as

x∈[1,4).

Question 3
?

What is the domain of the function f(x) given above?

a
x∈[1,5)
b
x∈(1,5]
c
x∈[1,4)
d
x∈(1,4]
e
x∈[1,4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) above is defined for values between x=1 and x=4.

  • Since there is a closed circle at x=1, this point is included in the domain.

  • On the other hand, because there is an open circle at x=4, this point is not included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

1≤x<4.

Using interval notation, we write this as

x∈[1,4).

question.worked_solution:
The function above is defined for values between $x=1$ and $x=4.$

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=1,$ this point is included in the domain.

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=4,$ this point is also included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

$$
1\le x\le 4.
$$

Using interval notation, we can write this as

$$
x\in [1,4].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

What is the domain of the function given above?

a
x∈[2,4]
b
x∈(2,4)
c
x∈[3,4]
d
x∈(1,4)
e
x∈[1,4]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function above is defined for values between x=1 and x=4.

  • Since there is a closed circle at x=1, this point is included in the domain.

  • Since there is a closed circle at x=4, this point is also included in the domain.

Therefore, the domain of this function is

1≤x≤4.

Using interval notation, we can write this as

x∈[1,4].

solution.reasoning: The graph is defined for every x from 1 through 4. Both endpoints are filled, so both are included. The domain is x\in [1,4], option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.worked_solution:
The function above is defined for values between $x=1$ and $x=4.$

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=1,$ this point is included in the domain.

1\le x\le 4.
$$

Using interval notation, we can write this as

$$
x\in [1,4].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/d2b5a3500e8e3adf2023a1bfb7fabcd27398b029b87f474d00ffb7ac76b90e2a.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary point was identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,2.5)$ | $2.5$ | $(2.5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points.  Also, the graph of $y=f(x)$ is concave up in $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ and $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/fde284c6bda2a0a9dba79a41348cf25ce7d5e5db8d2af996c577ceca721d5ab2.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/1daad2a8baabf38dabf1dfe5f8d7e0edf4f3ac8645145f2d0513fc2c59fc26e0.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\text{const.}$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $0$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $-$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from  $0$ to negative)  when we pass through $x=0$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=0$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$ 

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/7bef73fc655d0953a315bdd6f9524d0527e54c65453f3359059df7d43c444de7.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $+$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from negative to positive) when we pass through $x=3$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=3$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We don't know the exact value of ${g}^{′}(0)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangent to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈0$ is negative.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Sketching the Derivative of a Quadratic Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ below. Sketch the graph of $y=f'(x)$, the derivative of $f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/1fcbb5677ad7c8f630ccd7d194ef92f59fe3424d6bdb85e20f1ae522567b94ec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $f'(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f'(x) <             0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary point was identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |
| $f'$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is concave up in $(-\infty,\infty).$ So, $f''(x) >  0$ and $y=f'(x)$ is increasing.

Therefore, the graph of $y=f'(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/1567dcdd3dac0eb6b76b71e20466a77457a3d956c85be96048e5d3a94568c03a.png)

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, if we denote $g(x) = f'(x)$ then $f''(x)=g'(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y=g'(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the critical points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $g'(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $g'(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $g'(x) < 0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the critical points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=g(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty)$ |

| $g$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{not extr.}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |
| $g'$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x \approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25.$ At the inflection points, we have $g''(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y=g'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x\approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25.$

We don't know the exact value of $g'(1)$ and $g'(2.25),$ but from the graph of $y=g(x),$ we can conclude that at $x \approx 1$ and $x\approx 2.25$ the slope is zero and negative, respectively.

Therefore, the graph of $y=g'(x)=f''(x)$ may look as shown below.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $f'(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x) > 0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f'(x) < 0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below:

| $x$ | $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ | $\textrm{min}$ | $\nearrow$ |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, we are told that the function has an inflection point at $x = 0.5.$ So $f''(0.5)=0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y=f'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of $f'(0.5)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x = 0.5$ the slope is negative. Therefore, we get a point below the $x$-axis:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/5994a9139fbd1c530692a2fb40b2fb1b4b7bd0b34b2bf7ff7194390542748977.png)

observed_steps.name: Example: Sketching the Derivative of a Piecewise-Differentiable Function
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Sketching the Derivative of a Smooth Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice the following: 

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get $f'(x) <         0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,\infty)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\nearrow$ | $\textrm{max}$ | $\searrow$ |
| $f'$ | $+$ | $\textrm{undef.}$ | $-$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. Also:

- For $x \in (-\infty,-1),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is an increasing straight line. So, $y=f'(x)$ will be a positive constant on this interval.

- For $x \in (-1,\infty),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is concave down. So, $f''(x) <  0$ and $y=f'(x)$ is decreasing on this interval.

Additionally, we have a rapid change of the slope of the tangent line when we pass through $x=-1$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=-1,$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y=f'(x).$

Therefore, the graph of $y=f'(x)$ may look as shown below.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $\text{const.}$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $0$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $-$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from  $0$ to negative)  when we pass through $x=0$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=0$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$ 

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.
